summary: Describes COPS, a simple client and server model for supporting policy control over quality of service signaling protocols. Network devices ask a policy server for decisions and carry them out. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: COPS lets a network device ask a policy server what action to take and report what it did. The connection keeps request state so the server can later revise its decisions.

questions: how do routers get policy decisions
what is a pdp and pep
how does cops keep alive work
subtitle: A persistent client-server protocol for network devices to request policy decisions.

tldr.problem: Network devices need to apply policy decisions, but the policy rules may be managed by a separate server.
tldr.mechanism: A Policy Enforcement Point opens a persistent TCP connection to a Policy Decision Point, sends requests identified by handles and receives decisions in typed objects.
tldr.outcome: COPS defines the shared message and state-management protocol, while client-specific documents define each policy use. RFC 2748 is updated by RFC 4261.

today: RFC 2748 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2000. It has been updated by RFC 4261.

sections.title: The Policy Client and Server
sections.content:
COPS is a query-and-response protocol between a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) and a Policy Decision Point (PDP). An RSVP router deciding whether to admit a reservation is one example of a PEP. A device may also use a Local Policy Decision Point, but the remote PDP remains authoritative.

The PEP sends requests, updates and deletions; the PDP returns decisions. The connection is stateful: the PDP remembers requests until the PEP deletes them, and the PDP can send a new decision later for an existing request.
sections.plainLanguage: A network device asks a policy server for a decision and follows the answer. The server can later send a new decision for a request it still remembers.

sections.title: Headers and Self-Identifying Objects
sections.content:
Each COPS message has a common header followed by typed objects. The header carries a 4-bit version, 4-bit flags field, 8-bit operation code, 16-bit client type and 32-bit message length. The current version is 1, and the defined solicited flag is 0x1. Messages are aligned on 4-octet boundaries.

Each object has a length, class number and type. The class identifies the information, while the type selects its form. The RFC defines 16 object classes, including handles, contexts, decisions, errors, timers, client identification and message integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: A COPS message begins with a header that identifies its operation and client type. Labelled objects after the header carry the details for that request or decision.

sections.title: Requests, Decisions and Reports
sections.content:
The PEP opens a client type with Client-Open; the PDP answers with Client-Accept or Client-Close. A Request includes a client handle and a Context that describes the event, such as an incoming message, resource allocation, outgoing message or configuration request.

The PDP responds with a Decision, typically Install or Remove. The PEP can report success, failure or accounting information, and sends Delete Request State when a request no longer applies. The PEP chooses each handle, which must be unique on its TCP connection for that client type and explicitly deleted before reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: The device opens support for a client type, then sends requests under unique handles. It reports the result and deletes a handle when its request state ends.

sections.title: Keep-Alive and Reconnection
sections.content:
COPS uses a persistent TCP connection, with the PDP listening on port 3288. The PDP sets a keep-alive timer in Client-Accept. The PEP sends a Keep-Alive at a random time between one-quarter and three-quarters of the minimum timer interval, and the PDP echoes it.

If the connection fails, the PEP SHOULD try the primary or a backup PDP and SHOULD make local decisions while disconnected. When it reconnects, the PDP may request a state resynchronization. The PEP reissues its active state and sends Synchronize State Complete when finished.
sections.plainLanguage: The PEP and PDP send keep-alive messages to check that the connection still works. If it fails, the PEP can make local decisions and later synchronize state with a server.

sections.title: Message Integrity and Authentication
sections.content:
The Integrity object can authenticate messages, detect changes and prevent replay. It contains a key identifier, sequence number and keyed digest, and must be the last object in the message. All implementations MUST support HMAC-MD5-96.

Security is negotiated once per connection during Client-Open and Client-Accept with client type zero. Each side supplies the initial sequence number that the other side must increment for later messages. IPsec or TLS may also protect the connection; key maintenance is outside the protocol, though implementations must allow manual key configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared-key digest and sequence number let each side check who sent a message and whether it was changed or replayed. IPsec or TLS can also protect the connection.

sections.title: Client Types and IANA Registration
sections.content:
Client types identify the policy application carried in a COPS message. Values from 0x0001 to 0x3FFF require Specification Required registration; 0x4000 to 0x7FFF are for Private Use; and 0x8000 to 0xFFFF use First Come First Served assignment.

New object class and type values, as well as new context, reason, report, command and error codes, require IETF Consensus. A client-type extension document describes how that client uses COPS.
sections.plainLanguage: Each policy application needs a client-type value so messages can be interpreted correctly. The RFC assigns different registration rules to different value ranges.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: COPS protocol version; current version is 1.

fields.name: Message length
fields.desc: Header and object length in octets.

items.label: REQ
items.desc: PEP asks the PDP for a decision.

items.label: DEC
items.desc: PDP sends a decision to the PEP.

items.label: RPT
items.desc: PEP reports the decision result or accounting.

items.label: CC
items.desc: Either side closes a client type.
